items.item: Row-group pruning and page-index pruning are the same overlap check (query range vs. recorded min/max) applied at two different granularities, not two different algorithms — this topic's own code reuses the identical overlap logic for both.

items.item: Sort order doesn't change what statistics record (every row group still has a real min/max either way) — it changes how tightly those bounds cluster around the actual values a query asks for, which is the entire difference between 1 row group read and 10.

at.step: Reveal: the same query, shuffled, skips nothing

items.item: A bloom filter's false-positive rate is a property of its size relative to how many values were inserted, not a fixed constant — this topic's own filter is sized to match the specification's own 1024-block/26,214-insert example specifically so the measured rate can be checked against a stated number.

at.step: Reveal: the measured rate matches the spec's own number

items.item: A bloom filter complements row-group/page statistics rather than replacing them — it's the tool for exactly the case (high cardinality, no useful clustering) where min/max statistics give up.

items.item: Truncating a stored bound is a legitimate, spec-documented space optimization; the bug this topic reproduces is specifically a truncation that rounds the wrong direction, not truncation itself.

at.step: Reveal: a truncated max that silently loses data

items.item: A truncated-max bug produces silently wrong query results (a real row missing with no error), not a crash or a visible failure — which is exactly what makes this class of bug dangerous in production.

at.deep: Lab: a bug that costs real rows, not just time

items.item: This topic's bloom filter substitutes a SHA-256-derived hash for the specification's own XXH64; the first attempt (a hand-rolled FNV-1a hash) measured a false-positive rate over 10x the spec's stated figure, traced to poor upper-bit distribution on sequential keys — a real, found-and-fixed bug, not a hypothetical caveat.
Projection pruning (skipping a whole column a query never references) is the coarsest and cheapest of this topic's skipping tricks, applied before row-group statistics are even consulted.

The page index is only consulted for a row group that survived row-group-level pruning — this topic's own code only builds page statistics for the one row group that wasn't already ruled out, matching how a real reader avoids the cost of reading page-level metadata it won't use.

at.step: Reveal: the page index goes one level deeper

items.item: Every skip decision in this topic depends on the writer's own recorded bounds being true; nothing about the reader-side overlap check can detect a bound that's simply wrong, which is why the truncated-max failure is a writer bug, not a reader bug.
